issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Karim, a 40-year-old paramedic, had always prided himself on his calm under pressure, his ability to bring order to chaos. That changed irrevocably two years ago when his young son, Omar, was involved in a severe car accident. Karim was off-duty, enjoying a rare day off, when the call came from his wife. He rushed to the scene, arriving moments before the first ambulance. The sight of Omar's crumpled car seat, the mangled metal, and his son's small, still form, imprinted itself onto Karim's mind with a horrifying clarity. He was a paramedic, trained for this, but seeing his own child like that, he was just a father, overwhelmed and utterly helpless. He felt a profound, sickening terror as he watched his colleagues work on his son, a feeling that still grips him with the same intensity whenever the memory surges back.

Now, when Karim tries to recall the details of that day, the memory often returns as a full sensory reliving. He can smell the burnt rubber and gasoline, hear the frantic shouts of bystanders, feel the rough texture of the asphalt under his knees, all as if he is standing there again. Yet, strangely, there are frustrating memory gaps; he simply cannot remember the exact moments he pulled Omar from the wreckage, nor the first words he spoke to his wife when she arrived. It's a blur of raw emotion and fragmented images, punctuated by that recurring terror.

The aftermath of the accident and Omar's long hospital stay left Karim with a pervasive sense of failure. "I should have protected him," he often thinks, the words a bitter mantra. "I'm a paramedic, I save lives, but I couldn't save my own son from that." This gnawing belief that he had failed to protect his child led him to conclude that he couldn't rely on himself, especially when it truly mattered. He had come to believe that he was permanently changed for the worse, a broken version of his former self.

These beliefs permeated his daily life. At work, the very environment that once defined him became a minefield of triggers. The visible injuries or wounds on others, particularly children, can instantly transport him back to Omar's bedside, making his hands tremble as he tries to maintain his professional composure. The sharp, clean hospital or antiseptic smell, so ubiquitous in his profession, often brings a wave of nausea and a tightness in his chest, a visceral reminder of the sterile, terrifying days spent waiting for news of his son. Even casual reminders of victims, like a news report about a child injured in an accident, can send a jolt of anxiety through him.

Karim found himself constantly on edge. A sudden, unexpected touch from a colleague on his shoulder would make him jump, his heart racing, adrenaline surging. His concentration suffered; he struggled to focus on patient reports or team briefings, his mind often drifting, unable to hold a coherent thought. In public spaces, he instinctively sought out seats with his back to a wall, where he felt safer, able to see everyone entering and exiting, a small, unconscious ritual he performed for a sense of protection.

To cope, Karim developed a series of maladaptive strategies. He threw himself into work, picking up extra shifts, telling himself it was to provide for his family. In reality, it was a desperate attempt to keep his mind occupied, to avoid the quiet moments when the traumatic memories threatened to ambush him. "If I just keep busy, I won't have to think about it," he reasoned, but the constant overworking only left him exhausted and irritable. He also tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing away any intrusive images or thoughts whenever they surfaced, often muttering "No, not now" under his breath. This relentless avoidance of his own thoughts, coupled with his physical absence, created a growing chasm between him and his wife, who felt he was emotionally distant and unreachable. Their once close relationship now felt strained, marked by silence and unspoken resentment. He also started making excuses to avoid specific training sessions, particularly those involving pediatric trauma simulations, knowing he simply couldn't face those scenarios, which began to impact his professional development.

The increasing distance from his wife, the constant exhaustion, and the gnawing fear that his diminished concentration might lead to a mistake at work finally brought Karim to seek help. He dreaded the prospect of talking about the accident, fearing the renewed terror that would inevitably resurface, but the thought of losing his family and his career, combined with the relentless internal battle, had become unbearable.
